newsitem.title: ITALY: TENNIS-ITALIAN DAVIS CUP CAPTAIN PANATTA RESIGNS.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-ITALIAN DAVIS CUP CAPTAIN PANATTA RESIGNS.

text.p: Italy's Davis Cup captain Adriano Panatta resigned on Friday in a move that could jeopardise the team's world group semifinal against Sweden.
Panatta, whose squad scored a surprise victory over Spain in the quarter-finals in April, told a news conference he could not continue to work with the current Italian tennis federation.
"I will not go back on my decision. With this president and this federation, I will not be captain or technical director," Panatta, 47, said.
He said his resignation would take effect immediately.

Panatta, who won Italy's most recent Grand Slam title at the 1976 French Open, said he was pushed to step down after a row with federation president Paolo Galgani over the renewal of his contract as technical director.
"After the success against Spain, I honestly expected that the federation would extend my contract. But it didn't happen," Panatta said.
Panatta's resignation threw the future of Italy's Davis Cup campaign into confusion.
Diego Nargiso, a member of the squad which beat Spain 4-1 in Pesaro, said the players had talked about the situation and hinted that they might consider pulling out of the Davis Cup.
"We, the players, have talked and in the next few days will make our position known. We could even take decisions which would hurt ourselves," Nargiso said.

But Panatta said he hoped the progress Italy had made in the competition would not be wasted and the players would face Sweden in the semifinals on September 19-21. The other world group semifinal is between the United States and Australia.
"In my opinion it is the squad's duty to play," said Panatta, who took Italy to last year's Davis Cup semifinals where they narrowly lost to France after leading for most of the match.
He added he had no idea who would replace him. "I am a coach. That's all I do. I don't want to wage a political war with Galgani," he said.
Galgani, the powerful head of Italian tennis since 1976, has drawn much criticism both in the media and the federation recently for his management style.
Sport and Culture Minister Walter Veltroni sent a letter to Italy's Olympic Committee president Mario Pescante on Friday expressing concern over the situation.
"The recent developments in the world of tennis, up to the resignation of an esteemed coach and Italian champion, confirm the worries I have expressed to you on many occasions," Veltroni said.
Galgani, whose term as president runs until 2000, said on Thursday he did not want Panatta to go but refused to revoke his decision.
